metadata.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

problem_summary.summary: Find the deepest node that is an ancestor of both given node references; either target may itself be the answer.
problem_summary.input_output: Input: root and existing node references p and q with distinct values. Return the LCA node reference.
constraints: p and q are distinct and both exist in the tree

brute_force.explanation: Find a root-to-node path for p and another for q using iterative DFS, then scan their common prefix; its final node is the lowest common ancestor.
brute_force.correctness_idea: Both paths share exactly the nodes from the root through their LCA. After the paths diverge, they cannot rejoin in a tree, so the last common reference is the deepest shared ancestor.
brute_force.time_complexity: O(n) expected for two iterative searches and path comparison.
brute_force.space_complexity: O(n) auxiliary for the parent map and the two target paths.

optimized.explanation: Traverse once while recording each discovered node's parent, stopping after both targets are found. Put p and all its ancestors in a set, then climb q until it reaches that set.
optimized.correctness_idea: The first node on q's upward chain that also lies on p's ancestor chain is the deepest shared ancestor, which is the LCA by definition.
optimized.time_complexity: O(n) expected — one traversal and at most O(h) ancestor lookups.
optimized.space_complexity: O(n) auxiliary for the parent map and ancestor set.

edge_cases.case: One target is an ancestor of the other
edge_cases.handling: The ancestor target appears on the other target's chain and is returned.

edge_cases.case: Targets lie in different root subtrees
edge_cases.handling: Their common ancestor chain first intersects at the root or a lower branching node.
Both implementations use explicit stacks rather than Java recursion.
